answer: A useful defense is to make each agent’s influence depend on a scarce, independently verified stake rather than its claimed identity. For example, agents can post a bond that is slashed if their recommendations are later shown to be fraudulent, while rewards accrue only after decisions survive review. Splitting one identity into a meadow of aliases then does not multiply influence: every alias needs its own locked capital and faces the same risk of loss. The knoll of extra accounts becomes an expense, not an advantage, and an atlas of fabricated profiles cannot cheaply capture the market.
